glossary.desc: Supreme King of Great Kings — the paramount imperial title adopted by Gupta and successor sovereigns.
Great King — used by early Gupta rulers, feudatory kings, and regional monarchs.
Supreme Devotee of Bhagavān (Viṣṇu/Vāsudeva) — signature Vaiṣṇava sectarian epithet of the Gupta emperors.
Supreme Devotee of Maheśvara (Śiva) — Śaiva royal epithet used by Vākāṭaka, Maukhari, and Later Gupta kings.
Most Worshipful Lord — high imperial title paired with Mahārājādhirāja.
Princely Counsellor / Senior Imperial Cadre Officer in Gupta and post-Gupta administration.
Chief Commander / Magistrate of the Army and Justice.
Minister of Peace and War (Foreign Affairs & Royal Charters).
Provincial Governor administering a bhukti (province).
District Magistrate / Head of a viṣaya (district).
Province or administrative division (e.g., Puṇḍravardhana-bhukti, Tīra-bhukti).
District or territorial unit below a bhukti.
Tax-free royal land or village grant endowed to Brāhmaṇas or religious institutions.
Tax-exempt land gifted to Vedic Brāhmaṇa scholars.
Copper-plate charter recording an official royal land grant and privileges.
Perpetual endowment whose principal cannot be spent or revoked.
Keeper of Royal Land Records and Archives.
Leading householder / cultivating peasant-proprietor of a village.
Royal Messenger / Executor who conveys the king's oral command for a grant.
Chief Archivist and Accountant General.
Chief Chamberlain / Guardian of the Royal Palace Gate.
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces (also title borne by Pravarasena II's officers).
Vedic Horse Sacrifice performed to assert paramount imperial sovereignty.
The Southern Realm (Deccan and Peninsular India).
The Northern Heartland (Indo-Gangetic plains of North India).
Bearing the Garuda emblem — the imperial seal insignia of the Gupta Empire.
King of Poets — title celebrated for Samudragupta in the Allahabad Praśasti.
Awakening Being in Mahāyāna/mainstream Buddhist dedicatory inscriptions.
Ordained Buddhist monk.
Buddhist monastery or monastic university (such as Nālandā).
Sacred Buddhist reliquary mound or monument.
Dependent Origination — the core Buddhist teaching inscribed on relic scrolls and stūpas.
Victorious Royal Camp / Mobile Imperial Headquarters from which charters were issued.
For the religious merit of one's mother and father — standard dedicatory formula.

metre_guide.anuṣṭubh: Anuṣṭubh (Śloka) — 8 syllables per quarter-verse (pāda), 32 syllables per stanza; the classic epic & legal metre.
metre_guide.vasantatilaka: Vasantatilakā — 14 syllables per pāda (– – ⌣ – ⌣ ⌣ ⌣ – ⌣ ⌣ – ⌣ – –); stately lyrical & panegyric metre.
metre_guide.śārdūlavikrīḍita: Śārdūlavikrīḍita ('Tiger's Play') — 19 syllables per pāda; grand, majestic metre used for royal praśastis.
metre_guide.sragdharā: Sragdharā ('Garland-Bearer') — 21 syllables per pāda in three 7-syllable cadences; ornate courtly kāvya metre.
metre_guide.mandākrāntā: Mandākrāntā ('Slow-Stepping') — 17 syllables per pāda beginning with 4 heavy syllables; solemn & reflective.
metre_guide.pṛthvī: Pṛthvī — 17 syllables per pāda; rhythmic classical Sanskrit court metre.
metre_guide.indravajrā: Indravajrā ('Indra's Thunderbolt') — 11 syllables per pāda (triṣṭubh class).
metre_guide.upendravajrā: Upendravajrā — 11 syllables per pāda starting with a light syllable.
metre_guide.upajāti: Upajāti — 11 syllables per pāda blending Indravajrā and Upendravajrā cadences.
metre_guide.vaṃśastha: Vaṃśastha — 12 syllables per pāda (jagatī class) with alternating iambic rhythm.
metre_guide.mālinī: Mālinī ('Lotus-Garlanded') — 15 syllables per pāda starting with six light syllables.
metre_guide.śikhariṇī: Śikhariṇī — 17 syllables per pāda starting with ⌣ – – – – –.
metre_guide.śikharinī: Śikhariṇī — 17 syllables per pāda starting with ⌣ – – – – –.
metre_guide.hariṇī: Hariṇī ('Gazelle') — 17 syllables per pāda with rapid opening syllables.
metre_guide.āryā: Āryā — Moraic (mātrā) metre based on 4-mora feet (gaṇas), popular in Prakrit & Sanskrit epigraphy.
metre_guide.gīti: Gīti — Moraic metre of the Āryā family with symmetrical half-verses.
metre_guide.drutavilambita: Drutavilambita ('Fast and Slow') — 12 syllables per pāda.
metre_guide.puṣpitāgrā: Puṣpitāgrā ('Flowering Tips') — Asymmetric (ardhasamavṛtta) metre of 12 and 13 syllables.
metre_guide.maṇimālā: Maṇimālā ('Jeweled Garland') — 12 syllables per pāda with caesura after 6th syllable.

inscriptions.title: Allahabad Prasasti of Samudragupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A round, monolithic sandstone column. Beside Samudragupta's praśasti, it also bears two inscriptions by Aśoka as well as a number of mediaeval inscriptions, some of which are written between and over the lines of Samudragupta's inscription.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The last line of the inscription is 180 cm above the point where the column starts from its present pedestal.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, called eastern Gupta by Bhandarkar
inscriptions.provenance: The pillar was found, and still remains, in Allahabad fort. It was possibly moved here from Kauśāmbī by Firoz Śāh or another early Delhi Sultan.
inscriptions.summary: Allahabad Prasasti of Samudragupta (IN00001) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Samudragupta. Inscribed on a pillar crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 66-97 × 1070 cm), it is currently preserved at: in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Prayagraj (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 33 epigraphic lines and features 7 poetic stanza(s) composed in mandākrāntā, pṛthvī, sragdharā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Eran Stone Inscription of Samudragupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A squared red sandstone block, probably a fragment of a column with a square cross-section. Originally it was probably an architectural element, possibly (Cunningham, cited by Bhandarkar 1981:221) of the tempe of the colossal Viṣṇu.
inscriptions.layout_desc: A fragment. At least six full lines have been broken away from the top (a stanza and a half, with one pāda per line as in lines 7 to 24 (slightly different in 9-10); there may also have been a prose incipit before the first verse), an unknown number of lines lost from the bottom. The first few characters of lines 7 to 24 are destroyed, and from line 25 onward one pāda of verse is also lost from the beginning of each line. Since the extant area is roughly rectangular, the original inscription must have covered a reverse L shape, which implies a carved image of some sort in the top left corner. The layout needs to be cleared by autopsy.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered by Cunningham between 1874 and 1877. Found in Eraṇ, a short distance to the west of the ruined Varāha temple in which there is an inscription of Toramāṇa.
inscriptions.summary: Eran Stone Inscription of Samudragupta (IN00002) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Samudragupta. inscriptions.title: Nalanda Grant of Samudragupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A single copper plate inscribed on one side only. Found without an attached seal.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Damaged in lines 4 to 7, particularly 7. The inscription fills most of the surface of the plate, with some margin on the proper right. Inscribed area dimensions estimated on the basis of plate size.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, called eastern Gupta by Bhandarkar and "about the 6th century" by Agrawala (along with the Gaya plate)
inscriptions.provenance: Found in 1927-28 at Nālandā, north verandah of Monastery Site 1 near the copper plate of Devapāla. May be genuine or an ancient forgery/copy. At some point of its discovery the plates were chemically treated to remove patina. [Bhandarkar 1981: 224] says that according to [Ghosh 1939]-40 some portions had been more legible before this treatment. I see no such claim in [Ghosh 1939]-40; in any case, according to [Bhandarkar 1981: 225,] "the inscription had already suffered considerably in lines 4-6, and particularly in line 7 in the effacement of letters when it was examined, but after chemical treatment these lines, and especially line 7, developed actual perforations."
inscriptions.summary: Nalanda Grant of Samudragupta (IN00003) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Samudragupta. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 27 × 23 cm), it is currently preserved at: Indian Museum, Calcutta. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Eraṇ (Airikiṇa), Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 13 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Gaya Grant of Samudragupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A single copper plate inscribed on one side only. No raised rims. An oval seal is attached to the left edge, rotated 90° counterclockwise with respect to the inscription. About one quarter of the height of the seal overlaps the plate; the width of the whole object is an estimate based on this. The characters and the material of the seal both seem different than those of the plate, and the seal is probably a genuine one from Samudragupta's time, while the plate is thought to be a copy (or a forged document) produced in the early 8th century.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Some damage halfway down the proper left side, where there is also a crack, and another smaller one at the top edge near the end of the first line. The size of the inscribed area is estimated.
inscriptions.script_desc: Northern class, with some characters antique, others modern in form. Bhandarkar assigns the script to the 8th century, Agrawala to the 6th and believes the plate was made by the same forger(s) as %IN00003
inscriptions.provenance: Obtained by Cunningham at Gayā before 1883, circumstances not reported.
inscriptions.summary: Gaya Grant of Samudragupta (IN00004) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Samudragupta. Inscribed on a plate with attached seal crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 26.5 × 18 cm), it is currently preserved at: British Library, Ind. Ch. 046. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Gayā, Bihar. The Sanskrit prose text spans 20 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Mathura Lakulisa Pilaster Inscription
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The top and bottom sections are four-faced, while the middle is octagonal. One face of the top and bottom and five faces of the middle are well dressed, the rest are rough, hence Bhandarkar's reasonable assumption that it was a pilaster built into a wall rather than a free-standing pillar. The dressed side of the top bears a sculpted trident, and that of the bottom has a standing figure of a corpulent nude male (about 30 cm tall), probably Lakulīśa.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the five dressed faces of the central section of the pilaster, readable in horizontal lines across faces (with 3-4 akṣaras on each face) rather than as separate columns. The third of the five faces is badly abraded. Bhandarkar (1981:234-235) theorises that the pilaster was already built in (perhaps into the shrine mentioned in the inscription) when the text was incised, and he takes the end of the inscription to be the first half of an āryā verse, for the second half of which there was no room available.
inscriptions.script_desc: Northern class, early Gupta script, most characters indistinguishable from Kuṣāṇa script. Bhandarkar and Agrawala give no sizes.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in July 1928 by a dealer (illicit?) in antiquities, attached to a well in Cāṇḍūl-Māṇḍūl Bagīcī near the Raṅgeśvar Mahādev temple of Mathurā. He took it to his place, from where the police took it to a godown.
inscriptions.summary: Mathura Lakulisa Pilaster Inscription (IN00008) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Various / Dedicatory. Inscribed on a pilaster crafted of stone / sandstone, it is currently preserved at: Mathura Museum (No. 1931). Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Mathurā, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 17 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Udayagiri Cave 6 Inscription of the Time of Candragupta II
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A smoothed and countersunk panel on the façade of the cave, to the north (viewer's right) of the entrance. In the dimensions above (quoted from Agrawala), depth stands for the depth of sinking back from the rock face. Below the panel there are four sculptural niches; the panel is about as wide as one such niche, centred above the niches. The two reliefs below the panel are a figure of a four-armed Viṣṇu with two small wives or attendants, and a twelve-armed Mahiṣāsuramardinī. The carved doorway is flanked by two dvārapālas. There is also another (smaller) Viṣṇu to the south of the entrance, and a high relief of Gaṇeśa on the south side wall of the porch. The cave is on the eastern side of the hill, a little to the south of the village and almost on the level of the ground. It was named "Chandragupta Cave" by Cunningham and is now referred to as Cave 6.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription occupies the upper part of the panel.
inscriptions.script_desc: box-headed Central Indian variety of southern class
inscriptions.provenance: In the modern period first noticed by Cunningham in the mid-19th century.

inscriptions.title: Gadhwa Donation 1 of the Time of Candragupta II
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The stone was re-cut sometime after being engraved. The front has traces of 11 lines of writing, with about 13 characters each. These are illegible, but appear to be in the same alphabet as the preserved inscriptions and seem distinct from those. The back face, where the original pillar or block seems to have been cut in half, is rough. The ends of all lines on the proper left side, and the beginnings of all lines on the proper right side, are lost due to this cutting. The top two or three lines are also broken away, while the bottom is unscathed. The upper part of the right side bears two inscriptions of Candragupta II's time (%IN00010, 7 extant lines, the ends lost, and %IN00011, 8 extant lines, the ends lost). These two are not separated from one another except by punctuation. The lower part of the right side bears an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00030, 9 extant lines, the ends lost), separated from the earlier inscription only by a horizontal line. The left side also has an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00021, 9 extant lines, the beginnings lost), only found in 1890 by Cunningham after clearing away a lime coat under which it was hidden
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the upper part of the proper left side of the stone. The first two entire lines and the second half of the seven extant lines line have been broken away.
inscriptions.provenance: Found in 1871-72 by Bābū Śiva Prasād, built into the wall of a residential house in Gaḍhwā Fort (13 km west by south of Bārā and 2.5 km south of the village of Bhaṭgaḍh in Karchanā Tehsil of Allahābād District).

inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The inscription is on the back wall of Tawā Cave in Udayagiri, a little to the left as one enters. The cave's number is 7 according to Williams (1982) and Agrawala (1983) as well as the signboard on site in 2017, but 8 according to Willis (2009) and Wikipedia. It has no interior decoration save a lotus carved on the ceiling; the exterior has an unadorned doorway flanked by two dvārapālas.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The rock surface is damaged by peeling off, but the text is largely legible.
inscriptions.provenance: The inscription was discovered for scholarship by Cunningham between 1874 and 1877.

inscriptions.repository: in situ in Qutb Mīnār complex
inscriptions.support_desc: An iron pillar, described in the inscription as a dhvaja of Viṣṇu.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The bottom line is about 220 cm above the stone platform in its present location.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, eastern Gupta, close in many respects to %IN00001, but with very marked serifs.
inscriptions.provenance: First noticed by Prinsep in 1834. Presently in situ at the Qutub Complex in Mehrauli; original location (called Viṣṇupada giri in the inscription) unknown. Local tradition holds it was erected by Anaṅgapāla Tomara (early 8th century). [Fleet 1888: 141] records small metal pieces "like bits of bar iron" in its foundation which suggest the present location may in fact be the original one. However, Bhandarkar (1981:258-259) observes that the pillar may have been moved along with its original foundation, as was the Delhi Aśoka pillar. Bhandarkar (1981:58-61) further theorises that the original site of the pillar was along the Vipāśā and also summarises other opinions.
inscriptions.summary: Mehrauli Iron Pillar Inscription of Candra (IN00015) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Candra (Candragupta II). Inscribed on a pillar crafted of metal / iron (measuring 30-40 × 720 cm), it is currently preserved at: in situ in Qutb Mīnār complex. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Mehrauli (Qutb Complex), Delhi. The Sanskrit text spans 6 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Basarh Seal Legend of Dhruvasvamini
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: An oval terracotta seal with a single-line border around it. The top part shows a seated lion facing proper right, separated from the inscription by a faintly preserved horizontal line.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is in the bottom half of the seal.
inscriptions.provenance: Found by Bloch in excavations in 1903-04 at the village of Basarh (ancient Vaiśālī), Muzaffarpur District, Bengal (map of site on plate XXXI, adjacent to [ARASI 1903]-04:82). The seals were found in the Fort, at a depth of 3 metres, at the site where according to local tradition the palace of Rājā Bisāl once stood (detail map on plate XXXIII, adjacent to [ARASI 1903]-04:88). The seals were in a room 10 metres square without any doorways, so it was evidently a subterranean vault (or refuse pit). A total of about 720 pieces of clay, with over 1100 seal impressions (of about 120 varieties), were recovered. All or most of these clay pieces seem to have been presses on strings used to tie letters. Beside the principal specimen, two more specimens of this seal impression were found, both "broken and very indistinct" ([ARASI 1903]-04:107).
inscriptions.summary: Basarh Seal Legend of Dhruvasvamini (IN00016) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Queen Dhruvasvāminī. Inscribed on a seal / fragment crafted of clay / terracotta (measuring 4.5 × 6.3 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Basāṛh (Vaiśālī), Bihar. The Sanskrit prose text spans 4 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Mandasor Stone Inscription of Naravarman
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: See component data for measurements. Bhandarkar (1981) believes the stone was cut purposely and neatly after line 9, presumably for some new building purpose.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Campus dimensions show the width of the first fragment and the combined height of the two fragments.
inscriptions.script_desc: Mālwā variety of western Gupta alphabet
inscriptions.provenance: See component histories for discovery. Presently the two fragments are on exhibit together in the Gujri Mahal Museum of Gwalior (erroneously labelled as Mandsaur Inscription of Chandragupta II, which should be the label for [OB00058], adjacent in the exhibit). The edges of the slab, especially the top and bottom of the first fragment, have been smeared with cement obscuring parts of the inscription.
inscriptions.summary: Mandasor Stone Inscription of Naravarman (IN00017) is an epigraphic record from the Aulikara Dynasty (Daśapura) (c. 400–540 CE), associated with Naravarman. Inscribed on a block found in two fragments crafted of stone / unspecified, it is currently preserved at: Gujri Mahal Museum, Gwalior. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Mandasor (Daśapura), Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 14 epigraphic lines and features 22 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Bilsad Stone Pillar Inscription of the time of Kumaragupta I: Primary (north column)
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Bilsad Northern Stone Pillar of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.support_desc: The pillar is at the southwest corner of the eastern part of Bilsaḍ village (see ASIR_10, Plate 5 for a map). It is the northern member of the western pair in a group of four columns, probably remnants of the temple of Mahāsena mentioned in the inscription. The western columns are circular monoliths with copies of the inscription; the other pair (26 metres to the east) is square and bears no inscription. The height given for the pillar is for the extant finished portion; the top is broken off, while at the bottom there is a rough section of unknown length. The southern column of the western pair has a duplicate of this inscription (%IN00020), with the lines arranged differently, and the text mostly eroded to illegibility. The eastern pair consists of square columns, bearing images of Gaṅgā (northern column) and Yamunā (southern column).
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription of 13 lines is on the eastern side of the pillar. Agrawala (1983:26) provides a third dimension (4.5 cm), which is presumably the depth of a recessed panel on the column.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, western Gupta, with oblong box-heads
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1877-78 by Cunningham in Bilsaḍ (aka Bilsaṇḍa, Etah District, Aliganj Tehsil, UP; probably 28.240780, 79.952236, but [Goyal 1993: 131] sasys the village is 4 miles to the NE of Aliganj, which would be 27.518327, 79.208260, where a village named Mitaulia seems to be situated).
inscriptions.summary: Bilsad Stone Pillar Inscription of the time of Kumaragupta I: Primary (north column) (IN00019) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a column crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 48-51 × ~300 cm), it is currently preserved at: probably in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bilsaḍ, Etah, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 13 epigraphic lines and features 2 poetic stanza(s) composed in sragdharā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Bilsad Stone Pillar Inscription of the time of Kumaragupta I: Duplicate (south column)
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Bilsad Southern Stone Pillar of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.support_desc: The pillar is at the southwest corner of the eastern part of Bilsaḍ town (Eta, UP). It is the southern member of the western pair in a group of four columns, probably remnants of the temple of Mahāsena mentioned in the inscription. The western columns are circular monoliths with copies of the inscription; the other pair (26 metres to the east) is square and bears no inscription. The height given for the pillar is for the extant finished portion; the top is broken off, while at the bottom there is a rough section of unknown length. The northern column of the western pair has the primary specimen of this inscription (%IN00019), while the present specimen is mostly eroded to illegibility.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the eastern side of the pillar. It is in 16 lines, as opposed to 13 in the other specimen. Dimensions are not available. Bhandarkar (1981:268) gives the beginnings of the legible lines and notes that this duplicate has clarified some uncertain readings in the primary inscription. Cunningham (1880b:19) observes that the upper part is much injured and the seven middle lines are completely gone, but the last five lines are "in tolerable condition, and seem to correspond letter for letter with the last part of the northern pillar inscription." The eastern pair consists of square columns, bearing images of Gaṅgā (northern column) and Yamunā (southern column).
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, western Gupta, with oblong box-heads
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1877-78 by Cunningham in Bilsaḍ (aka Bilsaṇḍa, Etah District, UP).
inscriptions.summary: Bilsad Stone Pillar Inscription of the time of Kumaragupta I: Duplicate (south column) (IN00020) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a column crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 48-51 × ~300 cm), it is currently preserved at: probably in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bilsaḍ, Etah, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 16 epigraphic lines and features 2 poetic stanza(s) composed in sragdharā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Gadhwa Donation 3 of the Time of Kumaragupta I, GE 98
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The stone was re-cut sometime after being engraved. The front has traces of 11 lines of writing, with about 13 characters each. These are illegible, but appear to be in the same alphabet as the preserved inscriptions and seem distinct from those. The back face, where the original pillar or block seems to have been cut in half, is rough. The ends of all lines on the proper left side, and the beginnings of all lines on the proper right side, are lost due to this cutting. The top two or three lines are also broken away, while the bottom is unscathed. The upper part of the right side bears two inscriptions of Candragupta II's time (%IN00010, 7 extant lines, the ends lost, and %IN00011, 8 extant lines, the ends lost). These two are not separated from one another except by punctuation. The lower part of the right side bears an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00030, 9 extant lines, the ends lost), separated from the earlier inscription only by a horizontal line. The left side also has an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00021, 9 extant lines, the beginnings lost), only found in 1890 by Cunningham after clearing away a lime coat under which it was hidden
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the upper part of the left side of the block. The first half of each line and almost all of the first line has been broken away.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, eastern Gupta, probably the same hand as the other inscriptions on this stone

inscriptions.support_desc: A single copper plate the proper right half of which is lost. The dimensions above are those of the extant portion. The upper right corner of this was broken off and lost in the Calcutta Industrial Exhibition of 1906-07; this is reported to have contained the characters ma and ra which may have been part of the name of Kumāragupta ([Bandyopadhyaya 1909: 459).] Bandyopadhyaya also says he took photos of the plates in a less damaged state - no information on whether these photos are still around somewhere.

inscriptions.title: Mankuwar Buddha Image Inscription of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Mankuwar Buddha Image of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.support_desc: An image of a seated Buddha, "very perfect … with a headdress like that now worn by the Abbots in Bhutân. It is a plain cap, fitting close to the head, with long lappets on each side. The figure is naked to the waist, and clad below in a dhoti which reaches to the ankles. The eyes are half closed, as if in meditation." ([ASIR 10: 6).] No dimensions reported.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the pedestal, one line along the top edge, another along the bottom edge. The height given here is for the two lines combined; the top line is about 2 cm tall, the bottom is 2.5 cm tall.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, eastern Gupta closely resembling %IN00001
inscriptions.deco_desc: Between the two lines of text at the top and bottom of the pedestal, there is a carved wheel in the centre, "with a man seated in meditation on each side, and a lion at each corner" ([ASIR 10: 6).]
inscriptions.provenance: Originally found (according to [ASIR 10: 7)] in a brick mound, probably the site of a Buddhist monastery to the northeast of Maṅkuār, between five rocky hillocks called Pañc-pahāṛ. Moved from there to a garden belonging to the Gosāī of Deoriyā. Discovered in 1870 by Bhagwanlal Indraji (it is not clear whether Indraji found it in the mound or in the garden). [Goyal 1993: 147] spells the name of the village मानकुंवर. It is said to be 14.5 km southwest of Arail in the Allahabad District of UP. Arail today seems to be a part of Allahabad, and there is a Manakwar at 25.299862, 81.810082, roughly at the right distance and in the right direction from there.

Inscribed on a sculpture / Buddhist image crafted of stone / sandstone, it is currently preserved at: State Museum, Lakhnau. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Prayagraj (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 2 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Gadhwa Donation 4 of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The stone was re-cut sometime after being engraved. The front has traces of 11 lines of writing, with about 13 characters each. These are illegible, but appear to be in the same alphabet as the preserved inscriptions and seem distinct from those. The back face, where the original pillar or block seems to have been cut in half, is rough. The ends of all lines on the proper left side, and the beginnings of all lines on the proper right side, are lost due to this cutting. The top two or three lines are also broken away, while the bottom is unscathed. The upper part of the right side bears two inscriptions of Candragupta II's time (%IN00010, 7 extant lines, the ends lost, and %IN00011, 8 extant lines, the ends lost). These two are not separated from one another except by punctuation. The lower part of the right side bears an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00030, 9 extant lines, the ends lost), separated from the earlier inscription only by a horizontal line. The left side also has an inscription of Kumāragupta's time (%IN00021, 9 extant lines, the beginnings lost), only found in 1890 by Cunningham after clearing away a lime coat under which it was hidden
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the lower part of the right side of the block, below %IN00011 and separated from it by a horizontal line. The second half of each line has been broken away.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, eastern Gupta, probably the same hand as the other inscriptions on this stone
inscriptions.provenance: Found in 1871-72 by Bābū Śiva Prasād, built into the wall of a residential house in Gaḍhwā Fort (13 km west by south of Bārā and 2.5 km south of the village of Bhaṭgaḍh in Karchanā Tehsil of Allahābād District).

inscriptions.support_desc: An oval terracotta seal. The dimensions I give here are from Agrawala, while those of the inscription are from Bhandarkar. I assume that one is for the inscription, the other is for the object; alternatively, Agrawala may be in error (his numbers are the same as for the seal of Dhruvasvāminī).

inscriptions.provenance: Found by Bloch in excavations in 1903-04 at the village of Basarh (ancient Vaiśālī), Muzaffarpur District, Bengal (map of site on plate XXXI, adjacent to [ARASI 1903]-04:82). The seals were found in the Fort, at a depth of 3 metres, at the site where according to local tradition the palace of Rājā Bisāl once stood (detail map on plate XXXIII, adjacent to [ARASI 1903]-04:88). The seals were in a room 10 metres square without any doorways, so it was evidently a subterranean vault (or refuse pit). A total of about 720 pieces of clay, with over 1100 seal impressions (of about 120 varieties), were recovered. All or most of these clay pieces seem to have been presses on strings used to tie letters.
inscriptions.summary: Basarh Seal Legend of Ghatotkacagupta (IN00031) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Ghaṭotkacagupta. Inscribed on a seal crafted of clay / terracotta (measuring 6.5 × 4.5 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Basāṛh (Vaiśālī), Bihar. The Sanskrit prose text spans 1 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A granite boulder about 1.6 km east of Junāgaḍh, at the opening of a gorge that leads to a valley around the Girnār mountain. The inscription is on the southern face according to [Prinsep 1838b: 337,] and on the northwestern face according to [Fleet 1888: 57.] The same boulder holds 14 inscriptions of Aśoka (on the eastern side according to Prinsep) and the inscription of Rudradāman (on the western side according to Prinsep). The inscriptions of Skandagupta's time are hard to read because, apart from erosion, the engraving is irregular, the natural patterns of the rock obstruct some of it, while some portions of the rock surface were left blank because of their irregularity.

inscriptions.title: Kahaum Pillar Inscription of the Time of Skandagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Kahaum Pillar of the Time of Skandagupta
inscriptions.support_desc: The pillar is square to the height of about 140 cm (the width and depth dimensions above pertain to this section), then octagonal for about 190 cm. The next section, about 180 cm, is sixteen-sided, and the next again, about 65 cm, is cylindrical. The next 23 cm is square again (the sides are 45 cm long here), and finally cylindrical again for 12 cm. The total length of the shaft is thus about 610 centimetres. One face of the bottom section has an image of a naked man with a seven-hooded snake above his head (probably Pārśvanātha), accompanied by two kneeling figures, one male and one female. The capital is 130 cm in total length, consisting of a lotus bell topped by another square section with a naked figure on each face (probably Ādinātha, Śāntinātha, Neminātha and Mahāvīra). There is a metal spike at the top which apparently held a carved image.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the three northern faces of the octagonal section of the pillar; the bottom of the inscribed area is about 230 cm from the ground.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered between 1807 and 1816 by Francis Buchanan (Hamilton) in Kahaum/Kahaon/Kahanv (कहाँव, Deoria dist., U.P.; 26.263251, 83.859819) his survey of the provinces subject to the Presidency of Bengal. The pillar is next to an old well, two ruined temples and several tanks, all of which (along with the village) are atop a low but large (500 yards square) mound of brick ruin.

inscriptions.support_desc: A single plate, wider ("higher") in the middle than at the edges. The edges are in some spots thicker than the surface, but the plate was probably not fashioned deliberately thicker around the edges. It is fairly thick, but the engraving is deep and shows through the back in many places. There is no hole for a connecting ring, nor is there any trace of a seal soldered to the place.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Inscribed on one side only. Campus size estimated on the basis of photo.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1874 by Carlyelle, found in a small stream at Indor (Indrapura/Indrāpura of the inscription; Agrawala gives the modern name as Indorkheḍā), about 8 km NW of Dibhai in Bulandshahr District, UP. (Note that this is not the city Indore, but a small village, described as deserted in [Bhandarkar 1981: 308;] probably identical to Indaur on Google Maps, at 28.248558, 78.210860.)
inscriptions.summary: Indor Charter of the Time of Skandagupta (IN00035) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Skandagupta Kramāditya. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 20.5 × 14-15 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Indor (Indrapura), Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 12 epigraphic lines and features 2 poetic stanza(s) composed in indravajrā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Bhitari Pillar Inscription of Skandagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The pillar is monolithic, consisting of a square base of 2 metres or more in height, a circular shaft (to which the diameter given above applies) 4.7 metres long, and a capital about 1 metre high. The capital is a lotus bell, with a deep narrow socket that presumably held a metal spike that in turn held a sculpture. The upper part of the base is smooth; the lower part is roughly chiselled.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the eastern side of the smooth upper part of the base.
inscriptions.provenance: The pillar, but not the inscription, was discovered in 1834 by Tregear in Bhitarī, Ghāzīpur District, UP. The inscription was found by Cunningham after clearing away the earth from the lower section of the shaft.
inscriptions.summary: Bhitari Pillar Inscription of Skandagupta (IN00036) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Skandagupta Kramāditya. Inscribed on a pillar crafted of stone / sandstone, reddish, Chunar (measuring 72 × 770 cm), it is currently preserved at: in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bhitari, Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 20 epigraphic lines and features 12 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh, mālinī, puṣpitāgrā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Nalanda Seal Legend of Vainyagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.repository: probably in the Archaeological Museum, Nalanda
inscriptions.support_desc: A triangular fragment; the width figure above is for the base. The original seal was oval.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Contains five lines; the first with just one extant character, while the last seems complete. Any number of lines above the present first line may have been lost, as well as a device above the inscription. Given its similarity to other Gupta seals from Nālandā, the original may have held 8 lines. The text is in relief.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, mixing features of eastern (ma, la) and western (sa, ha) Gupta alphabet
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1927-28 during the excavation of Monastery site 1 at Nālandā along with %OB00044, %OB00046, %OB00047, %OB00048, %OB00049 and %OB00052. All these seals are clay impressions that seem to have been baked accidentally in a monastery fire.
inscriptions.summary: Nalanda Seal Legend of Vainyagupta (IN00038) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Vainyagupta. Inscribed on a seal, fragment crafted of clay / terracotta (measuring 5.4 × 5.7 cm), it is currently preserved at: probably in the Archaeological Museum, Nalanda. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Nālandā, Bihar. The Sanskrit prose text spans 5 epigraphic lines.

glossary.desc: Supreme King of Great Kings — the paramount imperial title adopted by Gupta and successor sovereigns.

inscriptions.summary: Sarnath Buddha Image Inscription of the Time of Kumaragupta II (IN00039) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a sculpture / Buddhist image crafted of stone / sandstone, Chunar, it is currently preserved at: Sarnath Museum. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Sārnāth, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 4 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in āryā.

inscriptions.support_desc: A slab of "rather good and dark sandstone" ([Fleet 1888: 80),] also described as a fragment ([Fleet 1888: 79).]
inscriptions.layout_desc: 24 lines of text.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1884 by a railway engineer whom Fleet had sent to take impressions of Yaśodharman's pillar inscription. The slab was built into the wall on the right-hand side, halfway down a flight of steps leading to the river at Mahādev Ghāṭ in Mandasor, opposite the fort.
inscriptions.summary: Mandasor Stone Inscription of the Silk Weavers (IN00040) is an epigraphic record from the Aulikara Dynasty (Daśapura) (c. 400–540 CE), associated with Various / Dedicatory. Inscribed on a slab crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 80 × 42 cm), it is currently preserved at: Gujri Mahal Museum, Gwalior. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Mandasor (Daśapura), Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 24 epigraphic lines and features 44 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh, drutavilambita, hariṇī, indravajrā, mandākrāntā, mālinī, upajāti, upendravajrā, vasantatilaka, vaṃśastha, āryā, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Varanasi Stone Pillar Inscription of the Time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Varanasi Stone Pillar of the Time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.support_desc: The base of the pillar is rectangular to a height of 72 cm, with four niches containing images which may be avatāras of Viṣṇu (see [Banerji 1945: 6] for descriptions). The next section, 14 cm high, is octagonal, and the next, 12 cm high, is sixteen-sided. The next 14 cm is circular and seems to be a pūrṇaghaṭa, described as a "base with foliage" in [Banerji 1945: 5.] The next and last section is 19 cm tall and is square and plain. No width/diameter data available; from the photo, the width seems to be a bit over 30 cm, which fits in with the size of the inscription. The niche above the inscription has a two-handed image holding a club and a discus.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on one side of the square base of the pillar.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1940-41 at Rājghāṭ, Vārāṇasī.
inscriptions.summary: Varanasi Stone Pillar Inscription of the Time of Budhagupta (IN00043) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Budhagupta. Inscribed on a pillar crafted of stone / sandstone, Chunar (measuring ~30 × 131 cm), it is currently preserved at: Bharat Kala Bhavan, BHU, Varanasi. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Vārāṇasī, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 4 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Eran Pillar Inscription of the time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Eran Pillar of the time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.support_desc: The monolithic pillar is on a pedestal 4 metres square, 23 metres to the east of the general line of the Eraṇ temples, about 800 metres west of the village. By its position it seems to be connected to the small double temple marked C and D in [ASIR 10: 87.] The lower part of the shaft is square to a height of 6 metres (width and depth dimensions above pertain to this section). The next section is octagonal for 244 cm. This is followed by the capital, consisting of a lotus bell 106 cm tall, an abacus 46 cm tall, and a square block 92 cm tall. The lower half of this block is plain, while the upper half bears on each face two lions sitting back to back. On top of this there is a two-armed male figure 152 cm tall, with a radiated halo around its head. The figure has two fronts and no back. One of the faces looks west towards the temples, the other east towards the town.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The bottom of the inscription is 1 metre above the pedestal, on the west side of the pillar (facing the temples).
inscriptions.script_desc: southern variety. The characters are larger and more loosely spaced in the first three lines, then seem to get progressively smaller, reaching a minimum in line 6.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1838 by Captain T.S. Burt of the Engineers.
inscriptions.summary: Eran Pillar Inscription of the time of Budhagupta (IN00045) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Budhagupta. Inscribed on a pillar crafted of stone / sandstone, red (measuring 87 × 1310 cm), it is currently preserved at: in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Eraṇ (Airikiṇa), Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 9 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in āryā.

inscriptions.title: Damodarpur Charter 2 of Budhagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A single copper plate. A seal is attached to the centre of the proper right edge. It is oval in shape (4.5 cm tall and 4.1 cm wide) and is weathered to indiscernibility, but seems to have had a legend similar to that of %OB00051.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Inscribed on both sides, but the verso is all but illegible because of corrosion. Inscribed area dimensions estimated from photo.
inscriptions.provenance: Found in 1915 in Dāmodarpur (Bangladesh, Dinājpur district) along with %OB00024, %OB00026, %OB00040 and %OB00051, while clearing away a mound of earth between two tanks.
inscriptions.summary: Damodarpur Charter 2 of Budhagupta (IN00046) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Budhagupta. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 18 × 10.8 cm), it is currently preserved at: Varendra Research Museum. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Dāmodarpur, Dinajpur, Bangladesh. The Sanskrit text spans 19 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Bihar Sharif Pillar Inscription 1
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: No detailed description of the column is available; the information here has been gleaned from Plate XVII in [ASIR 01]. The bottom of the pillar is broken off. The extant lower portion is octagonal and 175 cm long; above this there is an apparently circular shaft 221 cm long, followed by a square section (unless this bit is circular too)for a further 38 cm.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is on the octagonal section; this first inscription occupies four faces. Dimensions are estimated on the basis of the drawing of the pillar and the dimensions of the two inscriptions (%IN00047 and %IN00048) which together measure 40 by 104 cm.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered by E. L. Ravenshaw in 1839, at which time it was installed upside down on high ground a little to the west of the northern gate of the fort of Bihar (present Bihar Sharif). He was told that it had been moved here from in front of the same gate. Cunningham (in the early 1860's?) found it fallen where Ravenshaw had seen it erect. In 1871 it was moved in front of the Bihar Court House by A. M. Broadley, who is also responsible for a number of crude English inscriptions on the faces of the pillar not inscribed in antiquity (reported in [ASIR 11: 192-193).] It was subsequently used to support the roof of a house built up around it. At this time it was still installed upside down, with the bottom (current top) 8 lines completely hidden by woodwork. These used to be only available in Mitra's and Cunningham's eye copies. In 1927 the pillar was moved to the Patna Museum.
inscriptions.summary: Bihar Sharif Pillar Inscription 1 (IN00047) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Various / Dedicatory. Inscribed on a pillar / fragment crafted of stone / sandstone, red (measuring ~60 × 434 cm), it is currently preserved at: Patna Museum. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bihar Sharif, Nalanda, Bihar. The Sanskrit text spans 13 epigraphic lines and features 10 poetic stanza(s) composed in praharṣiṇī, upajāti, vaṃśastha.

inscriptions.title: Eran Pillar Inscription of Goparaja
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The top part of a pillar, converted into a Śivaliṅga. In addition to [IN00050], the pillar also bears an inscription of Śrīdharavarman, presently not in the corpus ([Mirashi 1955: 605-611),] and an illegible inscription near the top ([Mirashi 1955: 608),] possibly defaced when the pillar was turned into a liṅga. The lower section of the extant column is octagonal, then sixteen-sided, then octagonal again. A compartment above the centre of Goparāja's inscription features a seated man and woman who are presumably Goparāja and his wife. Three compartments (two of which are above two of the faces occupied by Śrīdharavarman's inscription) bear reliefs of horsemen. Above this, the pillar is sixteen-sided once again, then octagonal again. Further up, it is again sixteen-sided and fluted or ribbed, curving into a round top (which according to [ASIR 10: 89] was reshaped when the pillar was turned into a liṅga.) The part outside the liṅga base is 76 cm tall, but no separate lengths are available for the various sections.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription is at the top of the lower octagonal section of the extant part of the pillar, occupying three of its faces. The bottom line is about 15 cm above the ground ([Bhandarkar 1981: 352;] it is not clear what ground this may be, I suppose it means either the very bottom of the extant fragment, or implies that it has been fitted in a new base which allows the inscription to show). The inscription is weathered and damaged by the whetting of tools on the edges, but most of it is quite legible on the original stone.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1874-75 or 76-77 by Cunningham. It was found (and may still be) under some small trees near the left bank of the Bīnā, about 800 metres southeast of Eraṇ, halfway between Eraṇ and the village of Pehelejpur. The bottom part of the original pillar is lost; the extant top portion has been fashioned into a liṅga. It was probably broken naturally (perhaps after falling), as its bottom is rough. It was fitted into a pedestal, which was broken open in the 19th century to reveal Goparāja's inscription, most of which had been hidden by the pedestal. A new, shallower pedestal was then made for it, and was in turn removed in the 1950s, revealing Śrīdharavarman's inscription which had been completely obscured before this time.
inscriptions.summary: Eran Pillar Inscription of Goparaja (IN00050) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Goparāja (time of Bhānugupta). Inscribed on a pillar / fragment crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 45 × 175 cm), it is currently preserved at: probably in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Eraṇ (Airikiṇa), Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 8 epigraphic lines and features 4 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh, indravajrā.

inscriptions.title: Bhitari Seal Legend of Kumaragupta II
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.ms_name: Bhitari Metal Seal of Kumaragupta II
inscriptions.support_desc: An oval seal, pointed at the top and bottom. It is surrounded by a raised rim about 2 cm wide on average and 0.9 cm high. The back has two knobs about 1 cm in diameter, probably serving to attach the seal to another object such as a copper plate. It is an alloy consisting of copper, silver and gold, about 63, 36 and 0.4 percent respectively. (Billon is a generic term for a silver or gold alloy containing a majority of base metal, usually copper.) The upper section (slightly less than half of the whole and separated from the inscription by a double line) bears an image of Garuḍa in fairly high relief on a countersunk surface. He faces front, with outspread wings. He has a human face with thick lips and a Vaiṣṇava mark on his forehead. A hooded snake is coiled around his neck. A circle and a crescent - perhaps cakra and śaṅkha; or Sun and Moon according to [Sastri 1942: 66] and Bhandarkar - appear in the field to his proper right and left respectively. See [Bhandarkar 1981: 359] for some more details.
inscriptions.layout_desc: 8 lines of text, fully preserved. Campus size estimated from photo.
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered before 1886 in Bhitarī (Sayyidpur Tahsil, Gazipur District, UP) while digging foundations for a building.
inscriptions.summary: Bhitari Seal Legend of Kumaragupta II (IN00055) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a seal crafted of metal / billon (measuring 11.7 × 14.6 cm), it is currently preserved at: Government Museum, Lakhnau. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bhitari, Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 8 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Damodarpur Charter of Xgupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A single plate without raised rims. The upper corner of the proper left side is lost, and both sides are damaged in places by corrosion. A seal is attached to the centre of the proper right edge. It is oval in shape (5 cm tall and 4.1 cm wide), divided into two parts by a double horizontal line in relief. The upper side bears a trident in relief; the lower side is inscribed.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Inscribed on both sides of the plate. Campus size (for the recto face) estimated from photo.
inscriptions.provenance: Found in 1915 in Dāmodarpur (Bangladesh, Dinājpur district) along with %OB00024, %OB00026, %OB00040 and %OB00042 while clearing away a mound of earth between two tanks.
inscriptions.summary: Damodarpur Charter of Xgupta (IN00056) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Various / Dedicatory. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 16.2 × 9.8 cm), it is currently preserved at: Varendra Research Museum. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Dāmodarpur, Dinajpur, Bangladesh. The Sanskrit text spans 23 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Nalanda Seal Legend of Visnugupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.repository: probably in the Archaeological Museum, Nalanda
inscriptions.support_desc: A roughly triangular fragment, consisting of most of the bottom proper left quarter of the original oval seal. The extant part bears only text, no imagery. Size figures are approximate; all published sources give the lengths of the sides of the "triangle" as 3 by 2.5 by 2.375 inches. Height and width are my estimates from these figures.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Four lines of writing are preserved at the bottom of the seal. Campus size estimated from photo.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class with mixed eastern and western features

inscriptions.summary: Nalanda Seal Legend of Visnugupta (IN00057) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Viṣṇugupta. Inscribed on a seal / fragment crafted of clay / terracotta (measuring ~6 × ~7 cm), it is currently preserved at: probably in the Archaeological Museum, Nalanda. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Nālandā, Bihar. The Sanskrit prose text spans 4 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Gadhwa Donation 5 Possibly of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The stone was re-cut sometime after being engraved. It seems to have been a section of a square pillar split lengthwise into four. The present object is inscribed on both the faces that were originally on the outside of the pillar. Dimensions above are estimates based on the inscription campus data given in Fleet and Agrawala. [ASIR 10: 10] describes the object as two fragments, which were apparently found together and may have been rejoined by restorers since then, hence they are treated as a single object here. The fracture appears as a horizontal line through line 8 of %IN00058 and between lines 7 and 8 of %IN00059. These fragments may or may not originate from the same column as %OB00010; since no previous editor mentions the possibility in spite of the obvious relatedness of the inscriptions, there may be some trivial but unrecorded factor, such as a difference in the material, that precludes it.
inscriptions.layout_desc: 14 lines, with the beginnings of each line lost. There were probably no more lines in this inscription.
inscriptions.provenance: Found (with many other Gupta-period fragments, none inscribed) between 1874 and 1877 by Cunningham in Gaḍhwā, after pulling down a ruined wall to the north of a mediaeval temple.

inscriptions.support_desc: Cunningham ([ASIR 10: 53-54)] gives the cave the number 10; Agrawala calls it Cave 20. The cave is high up in the northwestern end of the hill, about 100 metres beyond the "Amrita Cave." It consists of several rooms separated by walls constructed of stone. According to Cunningham (ibid.) the inscription is on the rock face in one of the northern rooms, while Fleet ([Fleet 1888: 258)] says it is on a partly natural and partly artificial low arch, leading from the principal room to the next room towards the east. The inscribed area is irregular and apparently not set off from the surface in any way, hence dimensions are recorded for the inscription only. Cunningham (ibid.) also observes that the inscription is damaged at the edges due to chipping of the angular rock surfaces, which seems to imply that it is on the inside of an arch or doorway, through a wall whose thickness is the width of the inscription. Dimensions given above are those of the inscription.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Eight lines, intact except for some chipping at the edges. The inscribed area is an oblong with the lower right (proper left) corner missing, but this is the original shape of the inscription, not a subsequent break. The modern numerals 31245 are inscribed below the last line, as observed by Fleet but not (yet?) by Cunningham. The tops of these numerals are visible below puṇyam in the rubbing, and they seem to be Devanagari.
inscriptions.provenance: In the modern period first noticed by Cunningham in the mid-19th century.
inscriptions.summary: Udayagiri Jaina Cave Inscription of the Time of Kumaragupta I (IN00060) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a rock face crafted of stone / local (measuring 39 × 21 cm), it is currently preserved at: in situ. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Udayagiri Caves, Vidiśā, Madhya Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 8 epigraphic lines and features 5 poetic stanza(s) composed in indravajrā, rucirā, upendravajrā, vaṃśastha.

inscriptions.provenance: Discovered in 1930 near an old well while excavating a tank at Baigrām, Bogra (Baguṛā) district, Rājśāhi Division, Bengal (now Bangladesh). Another copper plate, found with it, was taken away by the coolies and presumably never recovered (but, according to [Sircar 1943a: 12] this may have been the Kalaikuri-Sultanpur plate, %OB00067). The plate was in the possession of the Gauḍa Research Society, Howrah in 1931-32, and is now in the Indian Museum of Kolkata.

inscriptions.title: Paharpur Charter of the Time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: The dimensions above may pertain to the inscribed area rather than to the whole plate.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Campus dimensions estimated from plate size. 12 lines on recto, 13 on verso; letter height is smaller on the verso, leaving an empty margin at the bottom. The writing extends almost to the edges of the plate at all other margins. A hole caused accidentally during the plate's recovery has damaged some letters of the penultimate three lines on the recto and the first three lines on the verso; there is also some damage to the left-hand margin (recto view).
inscriptions.provenance: Found by K. N. Dikshit on 29 November 1927 while excavating a great temple at Pāhāṛpur (sic in [Dikshit 1929]-30:59; Pahāṛpur in [Goyal 1993: 277),] Rājśāhi District, Bengal. Discovered in debris in the circumambulatory passage to where it had evidently fallen from a higher level along with bricks and mud. A hole was accidentally punched in the plate at this time, causing damage to the penultimate three lines of the recto and the first three lines of the verso side. It was covered with verdigris and has been cleaned chemically.
inscriptions.summary: Paharpur Charter of the Time of Budhagupta (IN00065) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Budhagupta. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 18.5 × 11.5 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Pāhārpur (Somapura), Naogaon, Bangladesh. The Sanskrit text spans 25 epigraphic lines and features 5 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Bhitari Inscription of the Time of Budhagupta, Front
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.repository: Dept. of Ancient Indian History, Culture and Archaeology, BHU
inscriptions.ms_name: Bhitari Stone of the Time of Budhagupta
inscriptions.support_desc: Probably a fragment of the rectangular section of a pillar, now itself in three fragments, found together and assembled. The present form is a squarish slab. The slab has one inscription (%IN00068) covering the front face (of all three fragments), and another (%IN00069) on the right-hand side (of the two right-hand fragments). Lines are entire in the front inscription, while on the side only the beginnings of lines remain. This suggests that the slab was cut (or has split) off the side of an original pillar of square cross-section. [Agrawala 1983: 111] says the side inscription is "apparently in continuation of the last line of the first side", but I see nothing that might warrant (or exclude) this, so I edit the inscriptions as separate. One fragment of the slab comprises the (viewer's) left-hand side, a bit more than half of the slab. The smaller right-hand portion is broken again in two; the location of this horizontal fracture is not described by Agrawala, but may be between lines 2 and 3 of the front inscription (%IN00068).
inscriptions.layout_desc: Inscribed all over the front face of the reassembled slab, consisting of five entire lines and traces of the top of a sixth (not reported by Agrawala). The beginning of the first line (which is almost certainly the first line of the original inscription) is lost and any number of subsequent lines may have been present after the sixth.
inscriptions.provenance: The three fragments were found (in the 1970s?) by K. K. Sinha during excavations in Bhītarī (at the site BTR 2), near Sayyidpur, Ghazipur district, UP.
inscriptions.summary: Bhitari Inscription of the Time of Budhagupta, Front (IN00068) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Budhagupta. Inscribed on a slab, broken crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 22.5 × 17.8 cm), it is currently preserved at: Dept. of Ancient Indian History, Culture and Archaeology, BHU. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Bhitari, Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit prose text spans 6 epigraphic lines.

inscriptions.title: Gunaighar Charter of Vainyagupta
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: [Bhattacharyya 1930: 45] describes the plate as "of good copper" so I have shown it as copper, not as alloy. A single plate, inscribed on both sides, thick and without rim. The surface is damaged in several places by hitting with a hard instrument; there is also corrosion damage. A seal, of a much lighter-coloured copper, is soldered to the (viewer's) left side of the plate. The seal is a slightly pointed oval about 10 cm wide and 12.5 cm tall (oriented 90° counterclockwise to the plate, i.e. the bottom of the seal faces the plate, and the longer diameter is along the longer axis of the plate). The seal is surrounded by a rim about 2 cm broad and separated by a double horizontal line across the middle. The top half bears an emblem of a bull recumbent to the proper right, in relief on a slightly countersunk surface. The bottom hald bears a corroded legend of one line.
inscriptions.layout_desc: 23 lines on the recto and 8 lines on the verso. Campus width is from [Bhattacharyya 1930: 45;] the height of the inscribed area is an estimate and applies to the recto face.
inscriptions.provenance: Found about 1925 in a tank in Guṇāīghar (or Guṇaighar?), about 3 km southwest of Debidwar in Tippera District, Bengal (now Bangladesh). Acquired as a loan by antiquarian Baikunthanath Dutt in 1928 and presented to D. C. Bhattacharyya for decipherment. Subsequent history not reported; apparently returned to private hands and not forthcoming.
inscriptions.summary: Gunaighar Charter of Vainyagupta (IN00070) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Vainyagupta. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper (measuring 25 × 16 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Guṇaighar, Comilla, Bangladesh. The Sanskrit text spans 32 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Sarnath Inscription of Prakataditya
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A stone slab that has been re-cut, leaving the top and bottom intact, but removing the (viewer's) right-hand side and possibly part of the left-hand side as well. There are also two round holes drilled into the surface at about half-height and 1/4 and 3/4 of the width.
inscriptions.layout_desc: The inscription of 16 lines covers the entire extant surface. The (viewer's) right-hand side, and perhaps a thinner slice of the left-hand side as well, have been cut away, resulting in the destruction of at least 18 characters per line.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, probably of the late 7th century, very similar to the Aphsad inscription of Ādityasena, but with some kuṭila features
inscriptions.provenance: Discovered by Cunningham in Sarnath, perhaps in 1861-62, but apparently not reported anywhere before [Fleet 1888]. Circumstances of discovery unknown.
inscriptions.summary: Sarnath Inscription of Prakataditya (IN00071) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Prakaṭāditya. Inscribed on a slab crafted of stone / sandstone (measuring 62 × 46 cm), it is currently preserved at: Indian Museum, Calcutta. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Sārnāth, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 16 epigraphic lines and features 11 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh, gīti, vasantatilaka, āryā.

inscriptions.title: Kalaikuri-Sultanpur Charter of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.repository: possibly at the Varendra Research Museum
inscriptions.ms_name: Kalaikuri-Sultanpur Plate of the Time of Kumaragupta I
inscriptions.support_desc: A single plate engraved on both sides. There is an oval projection in the middle of the (viewer's, recto) left side, to which a now lost seal would have been attached. There is a triangular hole in the centre of the oval. Judging from the indentation of the lines next to this area, the seal would have been about 8 cm in diameter.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Sixteen lines on the recto, eighteen on the verso, with both faces covered entirely by the inscription. The last line of the verso, containing the date, is squeezed into very little space and contains characters only in two places, near the centre of the line and near the end. The dimensions above are for any one face.
inscriptions.script_desc: northern class, similar to that of %IN00040 and other Damodarpur plates
inscriptions.provenance: Purchased in 1935 from a Muslim householder of Kalaikuri (Bogra District, near Naogong/Naogaon) and sent immediately to the Varendra Research Society of Rajshahi. Reportedly it had been kept in that Muslim family for a long time as an heirloom. [Sircar 1943a: 12] supposes this may in fact be the plate found together with the Baigram plate (%OB00055) and taken away by coolies. [Sanyal 1955]-56:57, however, reports that the Muslim family in question was living in Sultanpur (a suburb of Naogaon) at the time the plate was purchased from them, and had moved there two generations earlier from Kalaikuri when they inherited land there. He believes the family may have brought the plate along from Kalaikuri or may have obtained it there as part of their inheritance. He does not comment on Sircar's equation of the plate to the lost Baigram plate.
inscriptions.summary: Kalaikuri-Sultanpur Charter of the Time of Kumaragupta I (IN00074) is an epigraphic record from the Imperial Gupta Empire (c. 335–550 CE), associated with Kumāragupta I Mahendrāditya. Inscribed on a plate crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 24 × 14 cm), it is currently preserved at: possibly at the Varendra Research Museum. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Baigrām, Bogra, Bangladesh. The Sanskrit text spans 34 epigraphic lines and features 5 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.repository: in storage at Jhalawar Museum (acquisition number 63)
inscriptions.ms_name: Gangdhar Stela of the Time of Visvavarman
inscriptions.support_desc: Described as a tablet by Fleet, who probably only had access to a rubbing. The object appears to be a stela, basically rectangular in shape, with the top rounded into a circle (approximately 65 cm in diameter); the rectangular part is about 135 cm long and the neck where this joins the circular part is about 37 cm wide. The circular part is carved into a wheel of 16 spokes or, possibly, a lotus of 16 petals. Fleet believed this was a 16-leaved waterlily; the petals (or spokes) look like waterlily petals, but the centre (or the hub of the wheel) looks like the centre of a lotus. The longer (vertical) sides of the rectangular part are cut at an angle at both the front and the back, so this part is an elongated octagon in cross-section. The bottom is roughly worked and would have been hidden in a foundation. No description of the back side is available and it was not possible to lift the stone when it was examined in 2017. The fact that the sides are bevelled at the back just as they are at the front suggests that the stone would have been viewable from both sides as it was originally installed. The left edge and the top left and right corners of the inscribed area are chipped off.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Campus dimensions from [Fleet 1888: 72,] who erroneously says the larger figure is the breadth. The inscription consists of 41 lines. The left edge and the top left and right corners of the inscribed area are chipped off.
inscriptions.provenance: Brought to Fleet's notice in 1883 by Colonel W. Muir. In Gaṅgdhār (85 km SW of Jhalrapatan; now apparently in Mandsaur District, MP [unless it's Kota District, Rajasthan], shown on Google Maps as Gangadhar, 56 km east of Mandsaur). The stela was under a tamarind tree about 1.6 km north of the village, on the site of an old ruined temple. It was moved to Jhalawar Museum on 18 March 1917 according to the Museum's records, but according to [PRAS]-W_1906:56 it was removed from its original location in 1905-06, possibly to Jhalrapatan.
inscriptions.summary: Gangdhar Inscription of Mayuraksaka (IN00076) is an epigraphic record from the Aulikara Dynasty (Daśapura) (c. 400–540 CE), associated with Various / Dedicatory. Inscribed on a stela crafted of stone / unspecified (measuring 72 × 200 cm), it is currently preserved at: in storage at Jhalawar Museum (acquisition number 63). Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Gaṅgdhār, Jhalawar, Rajasthan. The Sanskrit text spans 41 epigraphic lines and features 25 poetic stanza(s) composed in mandākrāntā, vasantatilaka, śārdūlavikrīḍita.

inscriptions.title: Khoh Charter 1 of Hastin, year 156
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A set of two plates, each inscribed on one face only. Perforated about the middle of the upper side of each inscribed face and connected through the hole by a ring with an attached seal. The inscribed faces are presumably 1verso and 2recto, in which case the top of each page faced inward when the plates were opened like a book.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Dimensions estimated from plate size. 11 lines on each plate and a short legend on the seal.
inscriptions.provenance: Probably discovered shortly before 1848, perhaps by Colonel Sykes, in a valley near the village of Khoh (Google Map 24.365845, 80.719145), near the town of Uchaharā (Unchehara in Google Maps), presently Madhya Pradesh. However, [Fleet 1888: 100,] apparently relying on [Cunningham 1897: 7,] says the plates were discovered about 1852 by a Colonel Ellis. Apparently the plates later came to the hands of Major Kittoe, who presented them to F-E. Hall sometime before 1861, who gave them to the Benares College. At a later time (before 1888) they disappeared while being transferred from Benares to the Allahabad Museum and then on to the Provincial Museum of Lucknow.
inscriptions.summary: Khoh Charter 1 of Hastin, year 156 (IN00077) is an epigraphic record from the Parivrājaka & Ucchakalpa (c. 475–535 CE), associated with Mahārāja Hastin. Inscribed on a plate set crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring ~20 × ~13 cm), it is currently preserved at: lost en route to Lakhnau. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Prayagraj (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 23 epigraphic lines and features 3 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.title: Khoh Charter 2 of Hastin, year 163
inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A set of three plates, each inscribed on one face only. The plates are thin and deeply engraved, hence their backs were not suitable for writing on, as all details show through clearly. The third plate is much smaller than the first two, "evidently added as an afterthought, when it was found that the inscription could not be completed" (Fleet_1888:101). Each plate is perforated about the middle of the upper side and originally connected by a ring through the hole. The three plates together (without ring and seal) weigh about 500 grams. The inscribed faces are presumably 1verso, 2recto and 3recto, in which case the top of each page faced inward when the plates were opened like a book (and page 3 faced a blank page).
inscriptions.layout_desc: Dimensions estimated from the size of the first two plates. 13 lines each on the first and second plates, 4 more on the third. Well preserved except for a small piece broken away near the left side of the top edge of the third plate.
inscriptions.provenance: Probably discovered shortly before 1848, perhaps by Colonel Sykes, in a valley near the village of Khoh (Google Map 24.365845, 80.719145), near the town of Uchaharā (Unchehara in Google Maps), presently Madhya Pradesh. However, [Fleet 1888: 100,] apparently relying on [Cunningham 1897: 7,] says the plates were discovered about 1852 by a Colonel Ellis. Apparently the plates later came to the hands of Major Kittoe, who presented them to F-E. Hall sometime before 1861, who gave them to the Benares College. At a later time (before 1888) they were transferred from Benares to the Allahabad Museum and then on to the Provincial Museum of Lucknow. The connecting ring and the attached seal were lost during transfer, but the plates themselves reached their destination.
inscriptions.summary: Khoh Charter 2 of Hastin, year 163 (IN00078) is an epigraphic record from the Parivrājaka & Ucchakalpa (c. 475–535 CE), associated with Mahārāja Hastin. Inscribed on a plate set crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 19 × 14 cm), it is currently preserved at: Provincial Museum, Lucknow. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Prayagraj (Allahabad), Uttar Pradesh. The Sanskrit text spans 31 epigraphic lines and features 4 poetic stanza(s) composed in anuṣṭubh.

inscriptions.authority: Siddham - The South Asia Inscriptions Database
inscriptions.support_desc: A set of two plates, each inscribed on one face only. Thin and deeply engraved, hence the backs were not suitable for writing on. Perforated about the middle of the upper side and originally connected through the hole by a ring to which a seal was attached. The inscribed faces are presumably 1verso and 2recto, in which case the top of each page faced inward when the plates were opened like a book. The weight of the two plates (without ring and seal) is about 850 grams.
inscriptions.layout_desc: Dimensions estimated from plate size. 12 lines on the first plate, 9 on the second. A small piece is broken off the top left corner of the second plate; the rest of the inscription is in an excellent state of preservation.
inscriptions.provenance: Apparently ([ASIR 09: 7)] found in 1870 while ploughing a field belonging to the village of Majhgawam (Majgowa in Cunningham's spelling) in the valley around Khoh (Google Map 24.365845, 80.719145). The village is said to be about 3 miles to the SW of Uchaharā, but this appears to be the location of Khoh village; Google Maps shows several other settlements in MP by the name Majhgawan and Majhgawa, but none in this area.
inscriptions.summary: Majhgawam Charter of Hastin, year 191 (IN00079) is an epigraphic record from the Parivrājaka & Ucchakalpa (c. 475–535 CE), associated with Mahārāja Hastin. Inscribed on a plate set crafted of metal / copper alloy (measuring 22 × 15 cm), it is currently preserved at: unknown. Its historical provenance/origin is linked to Khoh, Satna, Madhya Pradesh.
